title: DAGs, Confounders & Colliders
interviewAnswer: A causal DAG encodes assumptions about which variables cause which others. A confounder causes both treatment and outcome and often needs adjustment; a collider is caused by two variables and conditioning on it can create a spurious association.
why: Choosing adjustment variables mechanically from correlation can bias causal estimates. DAG reasoning makes assumptions explicit before modeling.
intuition: Imagine arrows as information about the data-generating process. Conditioning can close useful backdoor paths—but can also accidentally open a path through a collider.
deepDive: The backdoor criterion formalizes sets that block noncausal paths between treatment and outcome without blocking the causal effect itself. DAGs do not prove assumptions; they make them inspectable.
workedExample: Ability → Training and Ability → Salary makes Ability a confounder when estimating Training → Salary. If Hiring ← Ability and Hiring ← Network, conditioning on Hiring can associate Ability and Network even if they were independent.
commonMistakes: Calling every correlated variable a confounder.
Conditioning on a collider because “more controls must be better.”
followUps: Can DAG structure be learned reliably from data alone?
production: For experimentation/decision systems, keep causal assumptions versioned alongside the analysis and distinguish pre-treatment from post-treatment features.

visual.caption: A confounder creates a backdoor path that often needs adjustment. Conditioning on a collider can create bias.
